title: A Satellite That 'Breathes' Air to Zoom Around Earth? Yes, Really!
summary:
What if a satellite could fly through the thinnest part of the atmosphere and use the air itself to keep moving—like a plane that never runs out of fuel? That's exactly what a Spanish company called Kreios Space is building. They've announced plans to launch the world's first air-breathing satellite thruster into orbit!

Here's how it works. Most satellites fly in low Earth orbit, about 100 to 1,200 miles up. They carry fuel to make small adjustments. But Kreios wants to fly in "very low Earth orbit" (VLEO), just 60 to 250 miles high. That's so low there's still a tiny bit of air, which creates drag and slows the satellite down. Normally, you'd need lots of fuel to fight that drag, and the fuel would run out fast.

Kreios's clever solution is called air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP). The satellite will scoop up the thin air around it, heat it until it turns into a hot, electrically charged gas called plasma, and then shoot that plasma out the back to push itself forward. It's like using the air as free, endless fuel!

"By enabling satellites to fly lower, longer and more efficiently, we are enabling higher-resolution Earth observation, much better satellite communications," said Kreios CEO Adrián Senar. The company hasn't set an exact launch date, but their website hints at 2027. They're working with a company called Kongsberg NanoAvionics to build the satellite bus that will carry the thruster. If it works, we could get sharper Google Maps, faster internet from space, and a cleaner orbit with less space junk.
why_it_matters: If this works, things like maps, weather pictures, and internet signals from space could get sharper and work better for everyone.

How high is very low Earth orbit (VLEO)?
What does the satellite do with the thin air?
options: Scoops it up, heats it into plasma, and shoots it out the back
Freezes it into ice and drops it
Uses it to cool the solar panels

options: The air creates drag that slows them down

Sharper Google Maps and faster internet

background_read: A satellite is a machine that circles Earth in space.
Most satellites carry fuel to keep them in the right orbit, and that fuel runs out.
Kreios Space (a Spanish company building the new thruster) is working with Kongsberg NanoAvionics (a company that builds the satellite body) to try a new air-fuel idea.
Article_Structure: WHO: Kreios Space, led by CEO Adrián Senar, is building the air-breathing thruster.
WHAT: The thruster will scoop up thin air, turn it into plasma, and use it to push the satellite forward.
WHERE: The satellites would fly in very low Earth orbit, about 60 to 250 miles above Earth.
WHY: Flying lower without needing much fuel could give sharper images, better internet, and less space junk.

perspectives.description: They see air-breathing propulsion as a way to make satellites cheaper and able to stay in orbit longer.
They worry that new satellites must still be designed carefully so they don't add more space junk.
They know the thin air at very low orbit is tricky, so the thruster must work for months in real space, not just on paper.
